issue: Does Honeycutt v. United States's bar on joint and several forfeiture liability apply to civil forfeiture under 18 U.S.C. § 981(a)(1)(C), so that imposing such liability is clear or obvious error under plain-error review?

sides.position: Honeycutt's limit on joint and several forfeiture liability applies to forfeitures under 18 U.S.C. § 981(a)(1)(C), so imposing joint and several liability is error. The excerpts do not identify which circuits hold this.
cases: Channon's acknowledged split (cited as United States v. Channon, 973 F.3d 1105 (10th Cir. 2020)) is the only source for this side; the excerpts do not name a circuit adopting it

sides.position: Honeycutt does not clearly or obviously reach § 981(a)(1)(C) forfeitures, given a split in authority, so the error is not plain and cannot be shown on plain-error review.
cases: United States v. Channon, 973 F.3d 1105 (10th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Cingari, 952 F.3d 1301, 1305–06 (11th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Dermen, No. 23-4074 (10th Cir. July 9, 2025)

this_court: does not decide the underlying question; it holds that any Honeycutt error under § 981 is not clear or obvious on plain-error review because of the acknowledged split (Channon), so the position that Honeycutt does not clearly reach such forfeitures controls at prong two
quote: observed “a circuit split has developed over whether Honeycutt applies to a forfeiture under 18 U.S.C. § 981(a)(1)(C).”
cite: United States v. Dermen, No. 23-4074 (10th Cir. 2025)
